# objection

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.objection.0)
[b4e3fa4e56d4b2fb] (h005.fork5.p.objection.0)
Source account: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: fcf00a2b164713c3af15c4067657244ca10281d69c6d2391cf552a3f450ec00c
Original body SHA256: 5cd8d521464e82577abd4dc580a53004973b48e07b0ed7d238eeb95cb8001ec3
Original commitments SHA256: 41b3083ded8c39f6ea59f4bc535b3681761d72b8647afd46957082299ae10aa4
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The account gives four facts worth separating: recurring arguments about chores; agreements that are later disputed in meaning; schedules that change; and one friend who has started avoiding the conversations. Each supports different conjectures.

First, the disputes are described as being about what an agreement meant, not about whether one was reached. That locates the failure between reaching agreement and remembering or applying it. Two mechanisms fit. One: the agreements were verbal and vague — 'I'll handle the bins' specifies no period, no trigger, no end date, so people can later reconstruct different meanings in good faith. Two: the agreements went stale when schedules changed, and reinterpretation is the face-saving way to exit an arrangement that no longer fits. These are not mutually exclusive — a schedule change gives everyone a motive to read an old agreement narrowly.

Second, there is probably no shared fairness criterion. Equal number of tasks, equal time cost, and equal exposure to unpleasant tasks are three different standards, and the account suggests none was ever made explicit. An 'agreement' under an unstated metric is underdetermined, which is exactly the kind of agreement whose meaning gets disputed later.

Third, changing schedules mean any fixed division is temporary. If the group's only mechanism for updating the division is a conversation, and that conversation has become aversive, the division will drift into stale resentment. The system needs a cheap routine way to be updated, not a better one-off agreement.

Fourth, the avoiding friend is the most informative fact and the least explained. 'Started' avoiding suggests something changed: the conversations may have begun to feel like blame; they may feel outnumbered by the other two; the chore talk may be a proxy for something else. Nothing available establishes which. The practical implication is sharp regardless: agreements negotiated by two people will not bind a third who was not there, so the repair path runs through re-including them at lower cost, not through deciding without them.

What follows practically, as proposals each attached to the conjecture it depends on:

1. Move agreements to a minimal written record, one line each: task, person, period, review date. 'Sam: bins, Sunday night, until the next review on the 15th.' This targets the vagueness mechanism. Its limit: if the disputes are strategic rather than sincere, the fight moves to the wording — but even then the disputes become concrete and small instead of diffuse.

2. Make the division explicitly schedule-sensitive: a short recurring review — ten minutes, fortnightly, or triggered by any roster change — whose only agenda is naming the fairness standard and re-dividing tasks given current schedules. This converts schedule changes from a silent invalidator of agreements into a routine event.

3. For the avoiding friend, lower the cost of re-entry rather than escalating the invitation. Asynchronous and written — 'here is a draft split for the next fortnight; mark anything you'd change' — before any face-to-face version. And once, separately, ask the direct question without an agenda attached: is it the chores, or how the conversations have been going?

4. A constraint on your own use of any record: do not let it become a prosecution ledger. A visible record used to win arguments will increase avoidance, not reduce it. Its job is shared reference, not evidence.

One caution directed at you: if past chore conversations have felt, to your friend, like tribunals, avoidance is a reasonable response rather than a character flaw. The account does not establish the tone of these conversations, but tone is the one variable you directly control.

If, once a record and a routine exist and the friend is re-included, the arguments continue at the same intensity, then the chores were probably never the substance, and the question shifts toward the living arrangement or the relationship itself — a different conversation, and one the account does not yet give grounds to open.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up involves several distinct commitments and exposes their tests.

Commitment to the recorded-agreement practice: one line per agreement (task, person, period, review date) in a place all three can see. This commits me to the claim that at least part of the 'disputed meaning' problem is a recording failure rather than a pure motive problem. If the flat already writes agreements down and still fights about their meaning, that conjecture weakens and the record proposal loses its point. It also carries a behavioral constraint I would be bound to: using the record as shared reference, never as evidence in arguments. Using it as a ledger against people would predictably deepen the avoidance and would count against the proposal.

Commitment to the recurring schedule review and to naming the fairness standard before dividing tasks. This commits me to the claim that stale agreements under changed schedules, plus an unstated fairness criterion, are real drivers of the arguments. Proposed test: whether 'who was supposed to do that' arguments decline once the division is current, written, and rests on a stated standard. If they do not decline, that claim weakens.

Commitment to the low-cost asynchronous approach to the avoiding friend, and to asking the direct question once about whether the problem is the topic or the conversations. This commits me to the conjecture that the avoidance is partly about format and cost. If the friend avoids the written, low-stakes version too, that conjecture weakens and the cause is more likely relational or substantive, in which case the method should change rather than be repeated harder.

Dependence I cannot escape: none of this is unilateral. The mechanism only works if all three accept it. I can propose, record, and moderate my own conduct, but cannot impose a system; if the others reject it, the open question becomes whether the division of work in this flat can be settled at all, and my proposals would not answer that.

Unresolved problems I am not claiming to have solved: the cause of the avoidance is not established by anything in the account; the group's actual fairness standard is unknown; whether the two non-avoiding flatmates are perceived as a bloc is unknown. I am also not asserting anything about whether the friendship itself is at risk or fine — the material does not say.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
